overview:
In Jain philosophy, "kashaya" (kaṣāya) refers to the deep-seated passions or emotional defilements that make the soul "sticky" to karmic matter and thereby perpetuate bondage in saṃsāra, the cycle of birth and death. Etymologically, some modern expositions gloss kaṣāya as deriving from roots meaning "worldly life" (kaṣa) and "gain" (āya), suggesting that as long as one harbors kashayas, one continues to "gain" worldly existence rather than liberation. More technically, classical Jain karma theory treats kaṣāya as a specific class of conduct-deluding (cāritramohanīya) karmas that shape the soul’s dispositions and intensify karmic bondage.

Across both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions, four principal kashayas are identified: krodha (anger), māna (pride or ego), māyā (deceit), and lobha (greed). These four are considered the primary passions that disturb equanimity, distort perception, and drive harmful action. They are called "sticky" because they function like glue, causing karmic particles (karma pudgala) to adhere firmly to the jīva (soul). When actions of body, speech, and mind (yoga) are performed under the influence of these passions, the resulting karmic inflow (āsrava) leads to long-term bondage (sāmparāyika bandha), determining future rebirths and obstructing spiritual progress.

Jain texts emphasize that kashayas are central among the causes of bondage. Tattvārtha Sūtra 8.1 lists five causes of karmic bondage: wrong worldview (mithyādarśana), non-abstinence (avirati), carelessness (pramāda), passions (kaṣāya), and activity (yoga). While yoga explains the inflow of karma, kaṣāya is singled out as the determinant of binding: because of passions, the soul attracts and assimilates karmic matter. Thus, even meritorious actions performed with subtle pride or greed can bind karma, whereas actions done without passions have only transient, minimal karmic effects.

Each of the four kashayas is further classified by intensity into four grades: anantānubandhī (extremely severe, binding endlessly and obstructing right faith and conduct), apratyākhyāna (severe, obstructing even partial renunciation), pratyākhyāna (moderate, obstructing total renunciation but allowing partial vows), and saṃjvalana (slight, obstructing perfect conduct while permitting initiation and progress). This sixteen-fold scheme (four passions × four intensities) is standard in Jain karma doctrine and is explicitly enumerated in Tattvārtha Sūtra 8.9. The more intense the passion, the heavier and longer-lasting the karmic bondage.

From the standpoint of ethical and spiritual practice, kashayas are seen as the greatest enemies of the soul. Anger (krodha) destroys forgiveness and peace, leading to violence and harsh speech. Pride (māna) inflates the sense of superiority and blocks humility and receptivity to truth. Deceit (māyā) creates a gap between thought, speech, and action, undermining straightforwardness (ārjava) and trust. Greed (lobha) fuels endless craving for possessions, status, or experiences, binding the soul like a heavy stone sinking in water. Jain teachers often group these into two broader tendencies: rāga (attachment), associated especially with māyā and lobha, and dveṣa (aversion or hatred), associated with krodha and māna. Both attachment and aversion are considered forms of delusion (mohanīya karma) that keep the soul revolving in saṃsāra.

The path of liberation in Jainism therefore requires the gradual weakening and eventual eradication of kashayas. Foundational practices such as right faith (samyagdarśana), right knowledge (samyagjñāna), and right conduct (samyakcāritra) are framed as ways to transform the inner dispositions that give rise to passions. Specific virtues are prescribed as antidotes: kṣamā (forgiveness) to counter anger, vinaya (humility) to counter pride, ārjava (straightforwardness) to counter deceit, and aparigraha (non-possessiveness) to counter greed. Meditative equanimity (sāmāyika), austerities (tapas), and mindful observation of one’s mental states (bhāvanā) are also emphasized as methods for witnessing and dissolving passions.

Jain texts and commentarial traditions stress that the mere suppression of outward behavior is insufficient if inner kashayas remain strong. A person may appear disciplined yet still harbor intense anger or greed, which continues to bind karma. Conversely, even laypersons who cannot undertake full renunciation can significantly reduce karmic bondage by softening their passions, cultivating forgiveness, and practicing honesty and contentment. Ultimately, the ideal of the Jina (Vītarāga)—the passionless conqueror who has completely transcended attachment and aversion—serves as the model. Liberation (mokṣa) is described as the state in which all kashayas and other deluding karmas have been fully destroyed, allowing the soul to rise to the siddhaloka, free from further rebirth.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra (Tattvārthādhigama)
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmi (accepted by both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions)
primary_sources.original_text:
अनन्तानुबन्ध्यप्रत्याख्यानप्रत्याख्यानसंज्वलन विकल्पाश्चैकशः क्रोधमानमायालोभाः ॥ ८.९ ॥
कषायो योगः कर्म बन्धः ॥ ८.१ ॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
anantānubandhyapratyākhyānapratyākhyānasaṃjvalana vikalpāś caikaśaḥ krodhamānamāyālobhāḥ || 8.9 ||
kaṣāyo yogaḥ karma bandhaḥ || 8.1 ||
primary_sources.translation:
8.9: The passions-feeling (kaṣāyavedanīya) karmas are of sixteen kinds: the four passions—anger (krodha), pride (māna), deceitfulness (māyā), and greed (lobha)—are each of four types: that which binds infinitely (anantānubandhī), that which hinders partial abstinence (apratyākhyāna), that which disturbs complete self-restraint (pratyākhyāna), and that which interferes with perfect conduct (saṃjvalana).
8.1 (as understood in standard commentaries): Wrong worldview, non-abstinence, carelessness, passions, and activity are the causes of karmic bondage.
primary_sources.notes: Tattvārtha Sūtra is a foundational Jain philosophical text recognized by both major sects. Chapter 8 deals with the bondage of karmas and systematically classifies deluding karmas, including kashayas. Verse 8.9 explicitly enumerates the four passions and their four intensities, forming the standard sixteenfold taxonomy of kashayas. Verse 8.1, together with its commentaries, situates kashaya among the principal causes of karmic bondage, highlighting its central role in Jain soteriology. The Sanskrit wording and numbering can vary slightly across editions, but the doctrinal content is consistent.

primary_sources.title: Sarvārthasiddhi (Commentary on Tattvārtha Sūtra)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Pūjyapāda (Digambara)
primary_sources.original_text: यः कषायवान् स आत्मनैवात्मानं हिंसति। अन्येषां प्राणिनां हिंसा भवति वा न भवति वा, तदनपेक्ष्यम्।
primary_sources.transliteration: yaḥ kaṣāyavān sa ātmanai vātmānaṃ hiṃsati. anyeṣāṃ prāṇināṃ hiṃsā bhavati vā na bhavati vā, tad anapekṣyam.
primary_sources.translation: "He who is possessed of passions (kaṣāya) injures himself by himself. Whether injury is then caused to other living beings or not is immaterial."
primary_sources.notes: Sarvārthasiddhi is a classical Digambara commentary on Tattvārtha Sūtra. In its discussion of kashayas, it emphasizes that the primary harm caused by passions is to the soul itself, regardless of whether external violence occurs. This underscores the Jain view that inner states such as anger and greed are intrinsically injurious and karmically binding, even if they do not manifest in outward acts. The passage is frequently cited in modern Jain educational literature to illustrate the ethical seriousness of kashayas.

primary_sources.title: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to early Śvetāmbara canonical compilers; individual authorship not specified
primary_sources.original_text: यथा महाशिलो तोये निमग्ना न पुनरुत्तिष्ठति, तथा कषायबहुलो जीवो संसारसागरान्नोत्तिष्ठति।
primary_sources.transliteration: yathā mahāśilo toye nimagnā na punar uttiṣṭhati, tathā kaṣāyabahulo jīvo saṃsārasāgarān nottiṣṭhati.
primary_sources.translation: "Just as a heavy stone, sunk in water, does not rise again, so the soul laden with kashayas does not rise from the ocean of saṃsāra."
primary_sources.notes: The Uttarādhyayana Sūtra is a key Śvetāmbara canonical text containing didactic verses on ethics and renunciation. The simile of the heavy stone vividly conveys how kashayas weigh down the soul and prevent its ascent toward liberation. While exact wording and chapter numbering differ among editions and translations, the image of the soul burdened by passions is widely used in Jain teaching to explain the practical urgency of reducing anger, pride, deceit, and greed.

primary_sources.title: Jainism Simplified (Community Educational Text)
primary_sources.author: Modern Jain educational authors (often anonymous or collective; not a canonical text)
primary_sources.original_text: The word kashaya (passions) can be broken down into kasha meaning worldly life and aya meaning gain. The literal meaning of kashaya is to gain worldly life again which means that as long as you have kashayas, the cycle of birth and death will continue.
primary_sources.transliteration: English prose; no original Sanskrit/Prakrit given.
primary_sources.translation: As cited: "The word kashaya (passions) can be broken down into kasha meaning worldly life and aya meaning gain. The literal meaning of kashaya is to gain worldly life again which means that as long as you have kashayas, the cycle of birth and death will continue."
primary_sources.notes: This modern explanatory text belongs to community education rather than primary scripture. It offers an etymological interpretation of "kashaya" that is pedagogically useful but not traceable to a specific canonical Sanskrit or Prakrit verse. It reflects the widely taught doctrinal point that kashayas perpetuate worldly existence, aligning with classical karma theory, but its linguistic breakdown should be treated as interpretive rather than philologically authoritative.

misconceptions.myth: Kashayas are just ordinary emotions like feeling annoyed or wanting nice things, and they only matter if they lead to obvious bad actions.
misconceptions.reality: In Jain doctrine, kashayas are not merely everyday moods but deep, passion-laden dispositions—anger, pride, deceit, and greed—that fundamentally distort perception and bind long-term karma. Even when they do not result in outwardly harmful behavior, their presence is considered intrinsically injurious to the soul and a major obstacle to liberation.

misconceptions.myth: Only monks and nuns need to worry about kashayas; laypeople can focus on external rules and rituals without addressing inner passions.
misconceptions.reality: Classical Jain texts present the reduction of kashayas as essential for all who seek spiritual progress, whether lay or monastic. While full eradication is associated with advanced stages of renunciation, lay practitioners are repeatedly encouraged to cultivate forgiveness, humility, honesty, and non-possessiveness as antidotes to anger, pride, deceit, and greed. External observances without inner transformation are seen as incomplete and still heavily karmically binding.

misconceptions.myth: Suppressing visible anger or greed is enough to remove kashayas, even if one continues to feel intense resentment or craving internally.
misconceptions.reality: Jain teachings distinguish between superficial behavioral control and genuine weakening of passions. Kashayas operate at the level of inner disposition; merely hiding or suppressing them does not prevent karmic bondage. Practices such as meditation, introspection, and cultivation of positive virtues aim to transform the underlying mental states, not just the outward expression.

misconceptions.myth: Kashayas are fixed personality traits that cannot be changed, so they are irrelevant to the practical path of liberation.
misconceptions.reality: Although kashayas are deeply ingrained, Jain philosophy holds that they are conditioned by deluding karma and can be gradually reduced and ultimately destroyed through right faith, knowledge, conduct, austerities, and meditative equanimity. The very structure of the sixteenfold classification by intensity presupposes that passions can be softened from extremely severe to slight and finally eliminated, making their transformation central to the path toward mokṣa.
